t.4.14.1: All of them went swiftly to Kiṣkindhā, ruled by Vālin, and, concealing themselves behind the trees, stood in the dense forest.
t.4.14.2: Casting his gaze in every direction across the forest, Sugrīva, lover of the woods and broad of neck, worked himself into a violent rage.
t.4.14.3: Then he, surrounded by his retinue, raised a terrible roar and challenged him to battle, as though splitting the sky with his cries.
t.4.14.4: Then Sugrīva, resembling the rising sun and moving with the gait of a proud lion, looked at Rāma, skilled in action, and spoke these words.
t.4.14.5: We have reached Kiṣkindhā, the city of Vālin, ringed by a net of monkeys, with gateways of refined gold, and rich in banners and war-engines.
t.4.14.7: Thus addressed by Sugrīva, the righteous-souled Rāghava, slayer of enemies, then spoke these words to Sugrīva.
t.4.14.6: O hero, the vow that you made earlier concerning the slaying of Vālin, make it fruitful quickly, as the season, when it has come, makes a creeper bear fruit.
t.4.14.8: Bearing this creeper named after the elephant as your mark of recognition, you look like the sun in the sky turned contrary to its nature, wreathed with a garland of stars.
t.4.14.9: Today, O monkey, with the release of a single arrow in battle, I shall free you from the fear and the enmity that have arisen from Vālin.
t.4.14.10: Show me Sugrīva's enemy, who bears the form of a brother, so that Vālī, struck down, may writhe in the dust of the forest.
t.4.14.11: If he, having come within the range of your sight, turns back alive, then you should not at once charge me with fault, nor should you reproach me.
t.4.14.12: Before your very eyes I split the seven sāla trees with an arrow; therefore you know that today Vālin is slain by me through my strength.
t.4.14.13: O hero, never before has a falsehood been spoken by me, even when I stood in hardship, filled as I am with a longing for dharma; nor shall I ever speak one in any way.
t.4.14.14: Cast off your agitation; I shall make my promise bear fruit, just as Śatakratu, with his rain, makes fruitful the rice that has sprouted in the field.
t.4.14.15: Therefore, O Sugrīva, for the purpose of challenging Vālin, who wears a golden garland, raise that cry by which the monkey will rush out.
t.4.14.17: Heroes who know their own valour do not endure the insolence of their foes in battle, especially in the presence of women.
t.4.14.16: Challenged by you, Vālī, flushed with victory, proud of his triumphs and fond of battle, will rush out of the city without hesitation.
t.4.14.18: Having heard Rāma's words, Sugrīva, tawny as gold, roared with a fierce cry, as if splitting the sky asunder.
t.4.14.19: Terrified by his roar, the cows run off, their luster gone, distraught like noble women assailed through the fault of the king.
t.4.14.20: The deer flee swiftly, like horses routed in battle, and the birds fall to the earth like planets whose merit has been exhausted.
t.4.14.21: Then the son of Sūrya, whose roar was like that of a mass of thunderclouds, his splendour heightened by valour, swiftly and confidently let loose a mighty roar, like the lord of rivers, the ocean, with its waves tossed by the wind.
